article.title: How to Replace a Rotted Deck Board
article.summary: Replace a rotted or cracked deck board: check the joists underneath, remove the fasteners, cut new boards to land on joists and screw them down.
article.body:
One soft or split deck board is a trip hazard and a sign to check what's underneath. Replacing a board is a few hours' work. This guide covers wood decks with boards nailed or screwed to wood joists.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: wear safety glasses and gloves. Set the circular saw depth to the board thickness so you don't cut into the joist. Treated lumber dust is irritating; wear a dust mask and don't burn the scraps.

Steps

  1. Check the joists under the board

    Before cutting anything, push a screwdriver into the joists under the damaged board and the boards around it. If the tip sinks in easily, the joist is rotted and needs repair first.

    Done right: the joists are solid, or you've identified which need a pro's repair.

  2. Remove the fasteners

    Back out screws with a drill. Pull nails with a cat's paw and pry bar, or cut them with an oscillating tool slipped between the boards if they won't budge.

    Done right: the damaged board is loose and the neighboring boards aren't damaged.

  3. Cut out the damaged section

    If only part of a long board is bad, cut it out so each new end lands over the center of a joist. If the cut falls next to a joist, screw a 2x cleat to the side of the joist to support the new board's end.

    Done right: every board end will rest on a joist or cleat.

  4. Fit the new board

    Cut the new board to length and brush end-cut preservative on any cut ends of treated lumber. Match the gap between boards: dry boards get about 1/8 in, while wet pressure-treated boards can be laid tight because they shrink as they dry.

    Done right: the board sits flat, its ends are tight to the neighbors, and the spacing matches the rest of the deck.

  5. Screw it down

    Drive two exterior deck screws at each joist, about 3/4 in from each edge, slightly below the surface. Pre-drill near board ends so they don't split.

    Done right: the board doesn't move or squeak when you walk on it, and no screw heads stick up.

Call a deck contractor if: the joists, beams, posts or the ledger board where the deck attaches to the house are soft, or many boards are failing at once. Those are structural safety problems.

FAQ

Can I replace just one deck board?

Yes. Remove the fasteners, cut the board so its ends land on joists, and screw the new one down.

What screws should I use for deck boards?

Exterior deck screws coated or made of stainless steel and rated for pressure-treated lumber.

How far apart should deck boards be?

Usually about 1/8 in for dry boards. Wet pressure-treated boards can go tight because they shrink as they dry. Follow the board maker's spacing for composites.

Will a new board match the old ones?

Not right away. New wood weathers over months; sealing or staining the whole deck helps it blend.
